projects.title: Blink & Beat
projects.goal: Build a working two-player reaction-time arcade game from a bare LED circuit.
projects.about: Project 1 exists to get every student building and coding something real in the very first session — no theory-first introduction, no 'intro to electronics' lecture. By the end of four weeks, every student has personally wired a circuit from individual components, written and modified real Arduino C/C++ code, and built a genuine two-player arcade game their family can play immediately.

projects.title: AgriBot
projects.goal: Build an automatic plant-watering system that senses real soil dryness and waters itself.
projects.about: Project 2 moves from digital (on/off) thinking to analog (a range of values) thinking, using a genuinely useful agricultural problem — knowing when soil is actually dry — as the vehicle. Students calibrate a real sensor against real soil, not an assumed number, and build a system that would genuinely be useful on a balcony, farm, or school garden.

projects.title: Health Guard
projects.goal: Build a wearable-style fall-alert device and a medicine-reminder box — two real health-tech ideas in one
projects.about: project. Project 3 introduces motion/tilt sensing and time-based reminders, both framed around a genuinely meaningful health application: helping an elderly family member or reminding anyone to take medicine on time. Students learn millis()-based timing (as an alternative to delay()) for the first time, a genuine step up in programming sophistication introduced because the project needs it.

projects.title: Smart Home Hub
projects.goal: Build a mini smart-home controller that automatically manages a light and a fan based on real light and
projects.about: temperature conditions. Project 4 introduces a second analog sensor type (temperature, via a thermistor) and combines it with the light-sensing skill already learned, teaching students to design a system that must weigh two different environmental readings and decide between them — a genuine home-automation problem.

projects.title: Park Assist
projects.goal: Build a real, driving robot car with an ultrasonic parking sensor and an automatic braking system.
projects.about: Project 5 is the course's first genuinely mobile robot. Students learn distance sensing, real motor-driver wiring (the single most important circuit-level electronics lesson in the whole curriculum), and build a physical chassis — culminating in a car that reliably brakes itself before a collision, just like a real automotive safety feature.

projects.title: Sentinel
projects.goal: Build a motion-sensing security alarm you can arm and disarm, just like a real home security system.
projects.about: Project 6 introduces a genuinely new sensor (a PIR motion sensor) and a new programming idea students haven't needed before — a simple state machine (armed vs. disarmed) — because a real security system must behave completely differently depending on its current mode, not just its current sensor reading.

projects.title: Clean City
projects.goal: Build a touchless smart dustbin with an automatic lid and a basic air-quality alert.
projects.about: Project 7 reintroduces servo control (last seen in Project 5's planning, now taught properly for the first time) in a genuinely satisfying context — a lid that opens by itself — and adds a gas/air-quality sensor, giving students their first experience with a sensor that detects something invisible in the air rather than light, distance, or motion.

projects.title: Guide Bot
projects.goal: Build a wearable-style assistive cane that alerts its user to nearby obstacles through vibration, not sound.
projects.about: Project 8 is CODE AI's most deliberately meaningful build: an assistive device for a visually-impaired user, using haptic (vibration) feedback instead of sound — a genuinely different actuator and a genuinely different design consideration (a device worn or carried by someone who needs to trust it completely).

projects.title: Rescue Alert
projects.goal: Build an early-warning device that detects rising water and gas leaks, with an escalating, tiered alert
projects.about: system. Project 9 combines a brand-new sensor (a simple DIY water-level probe) with the gas sensor from Clean City, and introduces tiered/escalating alerts — a genuinely important real-world disaster-management design pattern where a mild warning and a severe emergency should not sound identical.

projects.title: Mars Rover Challenge
projects.goal: Build an autonomous rover that follows a marked path and navigates around obstacles — then test it on
projects.about: unknown terrain on Mission Day. Project 10 is the grand-finale skills project, bringing together sensing, actuation, and decision-making into one autonomous rover framed as a Mars exploration mission. Students build line-following and obstacle- avoidance behaviour, tune a genuinely smoother proportional-control response, and finish with a 'Mission Day' where the rover faces a real, previously-unseen terrain layout for the first time — a celebratory, high- excitement event, not a graded exam.

projects.title: Capstone: Your Own Invention
projects.goal: Pick a real problem from any sector you've explored (or a new one), and build your own original
projects.about: invention from scratch. The Capstone hands full ownership to the student. Working individually or in pairs, students choose a genuine real-world problem — from health, agriculture, home, automotive, security, environment, accessibility, disaster-management, or any sector of their own choosing — and independently apply everything learned across all ten prior projects to design, build, and show off an original working invention.

capstone.good: A good Capstone idea: (1) addresses a real need, not just a convenient use of leftover parts; (2) is achievable in three weeks using skills and components from the course, plus a small, facilitator-approved addition if genuinely needed; (3) involves at least one real design decision the student can explain and defend; and (4) is small enough in scope that the student can explain every single part of it confidently at the Showcase.
capstone.ideas: A pet-feeder that dispenses food on a schedule; a smart study-lamp that reminds a student to take a screen break; a bicycle safety-light system with an automatic brake-light; a classroom door sensor that logs how often it's opened; an accessible doorbell with both a light and a vibration alert. Facilitators should actively welcome student-proposed ideas that go beyond this list — the more personal the problem, the better the final Showcase story.
capstone.timeline: Week 34: pick and clearly define your problem, plan your approach. Week 35: build a first working version, refine it based on your own testing. Week 36: finish, refine, and present live at the Final Showcase. There is no separate written report required beyond the student's own Build Log entries already kept throughout the project.
capstone.done: A student has completed the CODE AI Robotics Curriculum when they have built and demonstrated all ten flagship projects and a working Capstone invention, and can explain their Capstone confidently and honestly at the Final Showcase — including, where relevant, an honest note on what they'd still improve. That's the whole standard: built it, understands it, can talk about it. Nothing more, nothing less, and nothing that looks like a school exam.

sessions.title: Traffic Light (Blocks → Code)

fields.build: Build a working red-yellow-green traffic light in mBlock's drag-and-drop blocks, then see and rebuild the exact same thing in real Arduino code.
fields.components: Arduino UNO, breadboard, 3× LED (red, yellow, green), 3× 220Ω resistor, jumper wires, a computer with mBlock installed (free software, Arduino extension enabled).
fields.circuit: Red LED to pin 8, yellow to pin 9, green to pin 10, each through a 220Ω resistor to GND — identical wiring to Week 2 of the main course, deliberately, so it feels familiar later.
fields.stage1: In mBlock, drag out blocks to turn pin 8 on, wait, turn it off, then repeat for pins 9 and 10, wrapped in a 'repeat forever' block so the sequence loops continuously. Upload directly to the Arduino from mBlock and watch the real lights run.
fields.stage2: Click mBlock's 'Upload Mode' code view and look at the actual Arduino C++ it generated underneath your blocks. Find the line that matches your 'turn on pin 8' block, and the line that matches your 'wait' block — these are the exact digitalWrite() and delay() lines used throughout the main course.
fields.stage3: Open the real Arduino IDE for the first time. Using a lightly scaffolded template (setup() and loop() already written, a few lines left blank), type in the digitalWrite() and delay() lines yourselves to recreate the identical sequence you just saw generated — the point being made explicit: this is the same code, just typed by you instead of generated by blocks.
fields.codeReading: Compare your typed code side by side with mBlock's generated code and confirm they do the same thing, even if small details (spacing, variable names) differ.
fields.miniChallenge: Change the timing in mBlock first, re-check the generated code to see exactly which numbers changed, then make the identical timing change directly in the Arduino IDE.
fields.skills: Reading a real Arduino sketch for the first time, connecting a block to its underlying code, first hands-on time in the real Arduino IDE.
fields.buildLog: A quick note: what surprised you about seeing your blocks turn into real code?
fields.showFamily: A real, working traffic light the student built twice — once in blocks, once in real code — and can point to the exact lines that match.

sessions.title: Traffic Light + Buzzer Alarm (Blocks → Code)

fields.build: Add a buzzer alarm to the traffic light that sounds a warning during the yellow phase, and use a repeating loop for the first time in both blocks and real code.
fields.components: Everything from Bridge 1, plus 1 buzzer.
fields.circuit: Buzzer added on pin 11, alongside the existing three-LED traffic light wiring.
fields.stage1: In mBlock, add a 'repeat 5 times' block that beeps the buzzer quickly during the yellow-light phase, instead of writing five separate 'beep, wait' blocks one after another.
fields.stage2: Flip to the generated code and find the `for` loop mBlock created for your 'repeat 5 times' block — the same `for` loop used throughout the rest of this course to repeat an action without copy-pasting it.
fields.stage3: In the Arduino IDE, using another lightly scaffolded template, type your own `for` loop to make the buzzer beep exactly 5 times during yellow, matching what you just saw generated.
fields.codeReading: Trace through the `for` loop by hand and predict exactly how many times the buzzer beeps before running it, then check your prediction.
fields.miniChallenge: Change the loop to beep 8 times instead of 5, in mBlock first, then directly in the Arduino IDE, without any other change.
fields.skills: Using a repeat/`for` loop in both blocks and real code, connecting a 'repeat' block directly to its code equivalent.
fields.buildLog: A note on how many beeps you settled on and why.
fields.showFamily: A working traffic light with a pedestrian-style buzzer alarm, built in both blocks and real code.

sessions.title: Automatic Boom Barrier (Blocks → Code)

fields.build: Build a real sense-decide-act system for the first time: an automatic boom barrier that senses an approaching 'vehicle,' sounds a warning, lifts the gate, then lowers it again.
fields.components: Arduino UNO, breadboard, 1 HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor, 1 micro servo motor (as the barrier arm), 1 buzzer, jumper wires.
fields.circuit: Ultrasonic sensor Trig/Echo on pins 9/10, servo signal on pin 11, buzzer on pin 8 — the same three components (ultrasonic, servo, buzzer) that reappear later in Park Assist and Clean City, deliberately.
fields.stage1: In mBlock, build the logic visually: 'if distance is less than 20cm, sound the buzzer, move the servo to 90 degrees (barrier up), wait, then move the servo back to 0 degrees (barrier down).' Upload and test with a hand approaching the sensor like an oncoming car.
fields.stage2: Flip to the generated code and find the ultrasonic-reading section and the servo-control section — the same distance- sensing and servo-writing code used later in the main course's Park Assist and Clean City projects.
fields.stage3: In the Arduino IDE, using a scaffolded template with the ultrasonic and servo library setup already provided, type the if-statement and servo command yourself to recreate the identical barrier behaviour.
fields.codeReading: Given a sequence of simulated distance readings (100cm, 40cm, 15cm, 5cm), trace through the code and predict at exactly which point the barrier should lift.
fields.miniChallenge: Get the barrier to reliably lift for an approaching hand and lower again once the hand moves away, tested at least five times in a row.
fields.skills: Your first complete sense-decide-act system, built in both blocks and real code — the exact architecture every later project in the main course reuses.
fields.buildLog: A photo of your working boom barrier and a note on what 'sense, decide, act' means in your own words.
fields.showFamily: A real, working automatic boom barrier — like a toll gate or society entrance — built by the student in both blocks and real code, ready to begin Week 1 of the main course.

sessions.title: Your First Circuit, Your First Program

fields.build: Wire a real LED circuit from individual components and make it blink under your own code's control — your very first build.
fields.components: Arduino UNO, breadboard, 1 LED, 1× 220Ω resistor, jumper wires, multimeter.
fields.circuit: LED anode through a 220Ω resistor to Arduino digital pin 8; LED cathode to GND.
fields.experiment: Before touching a single line of code, build the bare circuit with just a battery, the LED, and the resistor, and use a multimeter to see the actual voltage and current flowing through it. Then briefly (with your instructor) see what happens if the resistor is removed — a clear, memorable reason resistors exist.
fields.activity: Assemble the LED circuit on the breadboard, then connect it to the Arduino instead of the battery.
fields.robotics: A robot, underneath everything, is a circuit controlled by a program. Before controlling anything with code, you need to understand the physical circuit you're about to control.
fields.engineering: Every component has real operating limits (an LED can only handle so much current) — a good builder respects those limits before writing any code.
fields.electronics: Voltage, current, and resistance — discovered from your own multimeter reading, not a formula on a page.
fields.codeIt: Open the classic 'Blink' sketch, upload it to your own circuit, and watch it run.
fields.codeConcept: pinMode(), digitalWrite(), delay(), and the setup()/loop() structure that every Arduino program uses.
fields.codeReading: Given the Blink sketch with the delay numbers blanked out, guess what three different values would do — then run each one and check yourself.
fields.writeIt: Modify the Blink sketch so your LED flashes an SOS pattern: three short flashes, three long, three short.
fields.miniChallenge: Get your LED blinking at exactly 2 blinks per second, calculating the delay values yourself.
fields.debugging: Your instructor will secretly break one student's circuit (LED backwards, or a missing ground wire) — use your multimeter to find it like a detective, not by guessing.
fields.skills: Circuit building, multimeter reading, your first Arduino upload, reading code line by line.
fields.takeHome: Sketch your circuit in your build log and write one sentence on what the resistor actually does.
fields.buildLog: A quick photo of your blinking LED plus one line: what surprised you today?
fields.showFamily: A real, working blinking-LED circuit the student built and wired themselves — and can explain.

sessions.title: Traffic Light Sequencer

fields.build: Control three LEDs in a coordinated sequence, and use a repeating loop to build a pedestrian countdown warning — your first taste of real timing logic and real repetition in code.
fields.components: Arduino UNO, breadboard, 3× LED (red, yellow, green) plus 1 extra LED (pedestrian warning), 4× 220Ω resistor, jumper wires.
fields.circuit: Red LED to pin 8, yellow to pin 9, green to pin 10, pedestrian warning LED to pin 11, each through its own 220Ω resistor to GND.
fields.experiment: Try different timing combinations for the yellow light and notice how a 3-second yellow feels 'broken' while a 1-second yellow feels right — timing changes how a system feels to a user, not just whether it works.
fields.activity: Wire all four LEDs and test each individually before running the full sequence.
fields.robotics: Real systems (traffic lights, elevator lights, robot status indicators) coordinate several outputs in a precise sequence — this is a foundational robotics skill.
fields.engineering: Sequencing and timing is itself a design problem: the same four LEDs can feel safe or dangerous depending only on the timing you choose.
fields.electronics: Driving multiple outputs at once from separate pins, and thinking about how much current the board can safely supply.
fields.codeIt: First refactor a repetitive, copy-pasted traffic-light sketch into clean, named custom functions like redLightOn(). Then build a pedestrian countdown: instead of writing five separate blink-and-delay blocks to flash the warning LED five times, use a `for` loop that repeats the same two lines five times by itself.
fields.codeConcept: Writing your own custom void functions and calling them from loop() — organizing code instead of repeating it. Then the `for` loop: repeating an action a fixed number of times without copy-pasting it, introduced here for the first time and reused constantly for the rest of the course.
fields.codeReading: A provided traffic-light sketch has a bug where yellow and green overlap for a split second — trace the timing on paper to find it. Then, given a `for` loop that flashes a light `for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++)`, trace through it by hand and predict exactly how many times the LED blinks before checking your answer against the real code.
fields.writeIt: Add the pedestrian countdown LED with its own `for` loop (five flashes, counting down) that must never run at the same time as the green light. Then independently change the loop so it counts down 8 times instead of 5, without changing anything else in the code.
fields.miniChallenge: Time a real traffic signal (or look up real durations) and match your sequence to it, including a countdown-style pedestrian warning.
fields.debugging: Fix a version where two LEDs were accidentally wired to the same pin — notice the symptom (both lights always match) before diagnosing the cause. Then fix a `for` loop that runs one time too many or too few (a classic 'off-by-one' bug) by tracing the loop's start and stop conditions.
fields.skills: Multi-output control, writing your own functions, using a `for` loop to repeat an action, timing-based debugging.
fields.takeHome: Time a real traffic light near your home and record red/yellow/green durations.
fields.buildLog: A short clip or photo of your working sequence, plus a note on what a `for` loop let you do that copy-pasting the same lines five times would not.
fields.showFamily: A working traffic-light-plus-pedestrian-countdown model with correct, safe timing.

sessions.title: Press-to-Play — Reading a Button Reliably

fields.build: Read a real pushbutton reliably, and discover — by seeing it happen, not by being told — why an unconnected input pin is a genuine electrical problem.
fields.components: Arduino UNO, breadboard, 1 pushbutton, 1× 10kΩ resistor, 1 LED, 1× 220Ω resistor, jumper wires.
fields.circuit: Button between pin 2 and GND with a 10kΩ pull-down resistor to GND; LED on pin 8.
fields.experiment: Wire the button with no pull-down resistor first and watch the Serial Monitor print random, flickering values even when nobody is touching it. Then add the resistor and watch the readings become rock-solid.
fields.activity: Build the 'floating pin' version first (see the fault), then correct it.
fields.robotics: A robot has to sense the world reliably before it can react to it — unreliable input is one of the most common real causes of robot malfunction.
fields.engineering: Debouncing: a mechanical switch is genuinely 'noisy' at the instant of contact, and good systems plan for real-world imperfection instead of assuming ideal components.
fields.electronics: Pull-up and pull-down resistors, and why a disconnected digital pin has no defined voltage at all.
fields.codeIt: Use the Serial Monitor as a live diagnostic tool for the first time — watch raw pin values change as you press and release.
fields.codeConcept: if/else statements, boolean logic, and Serial.begin()/Serial.print() for live debugging.
fields.codeReading: Given an if/else sketch controlling an LED from a button, predict the LED state for five press sequences before testing.
fields.writeIt: Write your own toggle logic — one press turns the LED on, the next press turns it off — using a variable that remembers state.
fields.miniChallenge: Make the LED visibly flicker from switch bounce on rapid presses, then fix it with a simple debounce delay.
fields.debugging: A toggle sketch 'randomly' skips some presses — diagnose this as a debounce problem using this week's floating-pin knowledge, not a logic problem.
fields.skills: Reliable digital input, boolean state logic, live Serial Monitor debugging.
fields.takeHome: Find one button-operated device at home and guess what you think happens electrically when it's pressed.
fields.buildLog: A note on what the floating-pin experiment actually proved that you couldn't have guessed from a textbook.
fields.showFamily: A press-to-toggle LED circuit the student can demonstrate and explain, with no flicker.

sessions.title: PROJECT 1 BUILD: The Reaction-Time Arcade Game

fields.build: Combine everything from this project into one complete, original two-player game — an LED lights up at a random time, and whoever presses their button first wins.
fields.components: Arduino UNO, breadboard, 1 LED, 1 pushbutton, 1× 220Ω resistor, 1× 10kΩ resistor, jumper wires.
fields.circuit: LED on pin 8; debounced pushbutton on pin 2, as built in Week 3.
fields.experiment: Run the finished game 10 times and record your own reaction times — you'll discover even your own reflexes vary more than you'd expect.
fields.activity: Assemble the final circuit and house it in a simple cardboard enclosure so it survives being played with.
fields.robotics: A complete system rarely uses just one skill in isolation — this game combines output, input, and timing into one coherent behaviour for the first time.
fields.engineering: System integration: the skill of combining previously separate working parts into one tested, working whole.
fields.electronics: Consolidating this project's circuits — output and debounced input working together in one build.
fields.codeIt: You're given a mostly-complete reaction-timer sketch (the random-light part is done for you) and complete the timing- measurement part yourself.
fields.codeConcept: random()/randomSeed() for unpredictability, and combining previously-learned if/else and function-writing into one program.
fields.codeReading: Trace the full sketch as a class and identify which part handles randomness, which handles input, and which measures time.
fields.writeIt: Add a 'too early!' detection: if the button is pressed before the light comes on, show a message instead of a time.
fields.miniChallenge: Run a class reaction-time tournament — best average over 5 tries, wins bragging rights.
fields.debugging: Swap Arduinos with a partner and debug a version with one hidden fault, without being told what it is — no code-copying safety net.
fields.skills: Full system integration, using randomness in a program, measuring elapsed time, debugging someone else's circuit.
fields.takeHome: Write a short 'how to play' guide for your game as if explaining it to a friend who's never seen it.
fields.buildLog: A photo of your finished, enclosed arcade game and your best recorded reaction time.
fields.showFamily: PROJECT 1 COMPLETE: a working, enclosed reaction-time arcade game the student built, wired, and coded — playable by the whole family tonight.

sessions.title: Reading the World in Shades of Grey — Analog Input

fields.build: Understand that the real world isn't just on/off, and learn to read a continuously variable signal for the first time.
fields.components: Arduino UNO, breadboard, 1 potentiometer, 1 LED, 1× 220Ω resistor, jumper wires.
fields.circuit: Potentiometer's outer legs to 5V and GND, wiper to analog pin A0; LED on pin 8.
fields.experiment: Turn a potentiometer while watching raw analogRead() values on the Serial Monitor — see the full 0-1023 range appear live, then use map() to rescale it and compare.
fields.activity: Wire the potentiometer as a voltage divider and confirm smooth, non-jumpy readings.
fields.robotics: Many real robot inputs — like soil moisture, which this whole project is about — aren't yes/no, they're 'how much,' and a robot needs to sense that range.
fields.engineering: Signal scaling: real sensors rarely output exactly the range you need, so remapping between ranges is a routine, essential skill.
fields.electronics: Variable resistance (a potentiometer as a three-terminal voltage divider) and how turning a knob changes a voltage the Arduino can read.
fields.codeIt: Print both the raw analog value and the mapped value side by side on the Serial Monitor.
fields.codeConcept: analogRead(), the map() function, and the idea of the Arduino chopping a voltage into 1024 steps.
fields.codeReading: Given a map() call, calculate by hand what three different readings should produce, then check your work.
fields.writeIt: Use the potentiometer to control an LED's blink speed entirely on your own.
fields.miniChallenge: Calibrate so the exact centre of the knob gives exactly a 1- second blink.
fields.debugging: A sketch reads a constant, unchanging value no matter the knob position — trace it to the wiper not being connected to an analog pin.
fields.skills: Reading analog signals, remapping ranges, comparative Serial Monitor debugging.
fields.takeHome: List three household devices with a knob or slider and guess whether they work in a similar analog way.
fields.buildLog: A quick note: why isn't 0-1023 always the range you actually want to use?
fields.showFamily: A dimmable/speed-adjustable LED whose behaviour changes smoothly as the student turns a knob.

sessions.title: Sensing Real Soil — Building the Moisture Sensor Circuit

fields.build: Wire a real soil-moisture sensing circuit from a probe and a resistor, and calibrate it against actual wet and dry soil.
fields.components: Arduino UNO, breadboard, 2-probe soil moisture sensor (or two nails/wires as a low-cost DIY probe), 1× 10kΩ resistor, a small pot of soil, water, jumper wires.
fields.circuit: Soil probe and 10kΩ resistor in series between 5V and GND, midpoint to analog pin A0 — the same voltage-divider principle as the potentiometer, now with soil as the variable resistor.
fields.experiment: Push the probe into completely dry soil and record the analog reading, then water the soil and watch the reading change live — students discover the actual wet/dry numbers for their own soil, rather than being handed a number.
fields.activity: Build the soil-sensing voltage divider and test it in at least two different real soil samples (dry vs. just-watered).
fields.robotics: This is the same voltage-divider idea from Week 5, just with real soil as the variable resistor — recognising that one underlying principle explains many different sensors.
fields.engineering: Threshold calibration: a system's 'correct' trigger point depends on its real deployment environment, and a good builder tests and tunes it rather than assuming a fixed number.
fields.electronics: Soil (with water in it) conducts electricity better than dry soil — moisture literally changes the resistance being measured.
fields.codeIt: Print live soil readings to the Serial Monitor while physically watering the soil, watching the number drop in real time.
fields.codeConcept: Reusing analogRead() and map() from Week 5, now applied to a brand-new real-world sensor.
fields.codeReading: Given a specific dry-soil and wet-soil reading, calculate what threshold value would correctly separate 'needs water' from 'fine.'
fields.writeIt: Write your own threshold-based decision: turn on an LED whenever the soil reading indicates 'too dry,' calibrated to your own soil sample.
fields.miniChallenge: Correctly detect the moment soil crosses from dry to watered, live, in front of the class.
fields.debugging: A sensor that reads identically in both wet and dry soil usually has a poor probe contact or a wiring mix-up — diagnose it using the same comparative method as the experiment.
fields.skills: Real-world sensor calibration, applying a known circuit principle to a new physical sensor, threshold-based decision- making.
fields.takeHome: Test a plant at home (if you have one) — does its soil feel dry or moist, and would your sensor agree?
fields.buildLog: Your recorded dry-soil and wet-soil numbers, and the threshold you chose and why.
fields.showFamily: A soil-moisture sensor that visibly reacts (LED lights up) the moment soil actually needs water.

sessions.title: PROJECT 2 BUILD: AgriBot — The Self-Watering System

fields.build: Complete a real automatic plant-watering system: when the soil sensor detects dryness, a small pump or valve (simulated with a motor/relay) activates to water the plant.
fields.components: Arduino UNO, breadboard, soil moisture sensor (Week 6), small DC water pump or a relay module with a toy pump/valve, motor driver or relay, tubing, small water reservoir, jumper wires.
fields.circuit: Soil sensor on A0 (from Week 6); pump/relay control pin on digital pin 7, powered through the driver/relay from a separate small supply if needed, with a shared ground.
fields.experiment: Test the complete system on a genuinely dry plant and time how long the system takes to bring the soil back to a 'watered' reading, adjusting the watering duration accordingly.
fields.activity: Assemble the full watering system: sensor in the soil, pump/relay wired to water delivery, all mounted around a real small potted plant.
fields.robotics: This is AgriBot's complete sense-decide-act loop: sense soil moisture, decide if it's too dry, act by watering — the same three-step pattern used in almost every reactive robot.
fields.engineering: Over-watering risk: a system that waters for too long or too often can actually harm a plant, so a real design must include a sensible watering duration and a cooldown, not just an on/off switch.
fields.electronics: Driving a small pump or relay from the Arduino safely, including a shared ground between the Arduino and any separate pump power supply.
fields.codeIt: Combine the Week 6 soil-reading code with new pump- control code into one program that waters only when genuinely needed.
fields.codeConcept: Adding a cooldown/timer so the pump can't re-trigger every single loop cycle once it has just watered — introducing a simple 'wait before checking again' pattern.
fields.codeReading: Trace through the combined sketch with a sequence of soil readings (dry, dry, just-watered, still moist) and predict when the pump would and wouldn't activate.
fields.writeIt: Add your own safety limit: the pump should never run for longer than a set maximum time even if the sensor seems stuck at 'dry.'
fields.miniChallenge: Demonstrate AgriBot successfully watering a genuinely dry plant and then correctly staying off once the soil is moist.
fields.debugging: If the pump runs constantly without stopping, check whether the moisture threshold is being read correctly after watering, or whether the cooldown logic is missing — a real 'my code technically works but the behaviour is wrong' lesson.
fields.skills: Full sense-decide-act system integration, safe actuator control, timer/cooldown logic, real-world safety-limit thinking.
fields.takeHome: Write one paragraph on what you'd change about AgriBot if it had to water three different plants with three different water needs.
fields.buildLog: A photo of AgriBot watering itself, with your recorded dry/wet threshold and chosen watering duration.
fields.showFamily: PROJECT 2 COMPLETE: a genuine automatic plant- watering system, calibrated to a real plant, that the family can rely on while on vacation.

sessions.title: Detecting a Fall — Tilt & Vibration Sensing

fields.build: Wire and read a simple tilt or vibration sensor, and use it to detect a sudden, sharp movement like a fall.
fields.components: Arduino UNO, breadboard, 1 tilt switch (ball-and-socket type) or vibration/shock sensor module, 1× 10kΩ resistor (if using a bare tilt switch), 1 buzzer, jumper wires.
fields.circuit: Tilt/vibration sensor between pin 2 and GND (with pull-down resistor if using a bare switch); buzzer on pin 8.
fields.experiment: Hold the sensor upright and gently tip it to different angles, watching exactly which orientation triggers a change — discover its real, physical trigger point rather than assuming it detects 'falling' in some clever way.
fields.activity: Mount the sensor so it can be tilted by hand, and wire the alert buzzer.
fields.robotics: Health-monitoring devices often rely on surprisingly simple physical sensors (a tilt switch, an accelerometer) rather than anything resembling 'artificial intelligence' — recognising a real fall from a simple sensor is itself a genuine engineering challenge.
fields.engineering: False positives and false negatives: a sensor that's too sensitive will cry wolf constantly (every small bump triggers an alarm), while one that's not sensitive enough will miss a real fall — a real design trade-off with no perfect answer.
fields.electronics: How a simple tilt switch physically works (a small ball rolling to complete or break a circuit) versus a vibration sensor's contact-based triggering.
fields.codeIt: Write a sketch that sounds the buzzer immediately the instant the sensor is tipped past its trigger point.
fields.codeConcept: Reinforcing digitalRead() and if/else from earlier projects, now applied to a genuinely different physical sensor.
fields.codeReading: Given a sketch with the sensor reading inverted (triggers when NOT tilted, due to a wiring choice), trace through why the alarm behaves 'backwards' and fix the logic.
fields.writeIt: Add a short delay-based 'are you okay?' grace period after a tilt is detected, during which a button press can cancel the alarm before it fully sounds — a real feature of genuine fall- alert systems.
fields.miniChallenge: Reliably trigger the alarm from an actual gentle 'fall' motion (tipping the sensor sharply) without triggering from normal handling.
fields.debugging: An alarm that goes off constantly, even when the sensor sits still, usually has a floating-pin problem — apply the Project 1 pull-down-resistor lesson to a brand-new sensor.
fields.skills: New sensor type integration, false-positive/false-negative trade-off reasoning, grace-period/cancel logic.
fields.takeHome: Ask a family member what would actually make them trust (or not trust) a fall-alert device, and record their honest answer.
fields.buildLog: A note on the exact tilt angle that triggers your sensor, and whether that felt too sensitive or not sensitive enough.
fields.showFamily: A working tilt-triggered alarm the student can demonstrate, including the 'are you okay?' cancel feature.

sessions.title: The Medicine Reminder — Timing Without delay()

fields.build: Build a periodic reminder system using millis() instead of delay(), so the Arduino can keep sensing while also tracking time in the background.
fields.components: Arduino UNO, breadboard, 1 buzzer, 1 LED, 1 pushbutton (to acknowledge/dismiss the reminder), jumper wires.
fields.circuit: Buzzer on pin 8, LED on pin 9, button on pin 2 (reused from Project 1's debounced button wiring).
fields.experiment: Compare a delay()-based blink (which freezes everything else while waiting) against a millis()-based blink (which lets a button still be checked at the same time) by trying to press a button during each — students feel the difference directly rather than being told about it.
fields.activity: Wire the reminder buzzer/LED and the acknowledge button on the same board.
fields.robotics: A real device (like a medicine reminder, or any robot that must sense continuously) usually cannot afford to 'freeze' while waiting for a timer — it needs to track time while still doing other things.
fields.engineering: Concurrency-lite: doing two things that both depend on time (waiting for a reminder AND checking a button) without one blocking the other, a genuinely important real-world engineering idea introduced here in its simplest possible form.
fields.electronics: No new wiring concept — full reuse of prior buzzer/LED/button wiring, with the week's focus kept entirely on the code side.
fields.codeIt: Convert a working delay()-based reminder sketch into a millis()-based one, and verify the button now works even while the buzzer 'countdown' is running.
fields.codeConcept: millis() as the Arduino's built-in stopwatch, and the 'if enough time has passed, do the thing' pattern that replaces delay() when you need to do more than one thing at once.
fields.codeReading: Given a millis()-based sketch, calculate by hand exactly when (in milliseconds) the next reminder will fire, given a start time and interval.
fields.writeIt: Independently add a second, longer-interval reminder (e.g., a 'take your evening medicine' reminder alongside a 'morning medicine' one) using two independent millis() timers.
fields.miniChallenge: Successfully dismiss a reminder with the button before it repeats, and confirm the timer correctly resets.
fields.debugging: A common millis() bug is comparing time incorrectly and never triggering, or triggering every single loop — trace through the actual millis() values printed to Serial Monitor to find the error.
fields.skills: Non-blocking timing with millis(), running two independent behaviours at once, real-time debugging using Serial Monitor timestamps.
fields.takeHome: List two other real devices you think use a 'do something every X minutes' pattern (a washing machine, a traffic light, a phone reminder).
fields.buildLog: A note explaining, in your own words, why delay() would have been a worse choice for this project than millis().
fields.showFamily: A working medicine-reminder box that beeps on schedule and can be acknowledged with a button press.

sessions.title: PROJECT 3 BUILD: Health Guard — Fall Alert + Medicine Reminder

fields.build: Combine the fall-detection sensor and the millis()-based reminder system into one complete Health Guard device.
fields.components: Tilt/vibration sensor (Week 8), buzzer, LED, pushbutton, Arduino UNO, breadboard, jumper wires.
fields.circuit: Full combination of Weeks 8 and 9 wiring on one board, with a documented pin map since the system now uses more pins than any single previous week.
fields.experiment: Test the combined device under realistic conditions: a genuine 'fall' motion during a reminder countdown, confirming the fall alert correctly interrupts and takes priority over a routine reminder.
fields.activity: Final assembly of both subsystems into one small enclosure, wired to share the Arduino without pin conflicts.
fields.robotics: Health Guard is this project's full integration: two independent behaviours (scheduled reminders and emergency fall detection) running on the same device, with one correctly taking priority over the other when both occur.
fields.engineering: Priority resolution: when two things could both want the buzzer at once (a routine reminder and an emergency fall alert), a good design must explicitly decide, and justify, which one wins — the same kind of decision a real safety- critical device must make.
fields.electronics: Full consolidation of buzzer, LED, tilt-sensor, and button wiring on a single shared board with a clean, documented pin map.
fields.codeIt: Merge the Week 8 and Week 9 sketches into one combined program, resolving which subsystem takes priority when both are active.
fields.codeConcept: Consolidation of millis()-based timing and digitalRead()- based sensing into one well-organized combined program.
fields.codeReading: Trace through the combined code for a specific scenario (a fall occurs exactly during a reminder countdown) and confirm, on paper, what the code should do before testing it live.
fields.writeIt: Independently design and implement your own priority rule for what happens if the fall alert and a reminder genuinely coincide, and be ready to explain your choice.
fields.miniChallenge: Demonstrate Health Guard correctly handling both a routine reminder and a simulated fall, live, in front of the class.
fields.debugging: If combining the two subsystems breaks one of them, use the Project 1 debugging habit (isolate before you fix) to find out exactly which new line caused the regression.
fields.skills: Multi-subsystem integration, priority/conflict resolution design, real health-tech safety-first thinking.
fields.takeHome: Write half a page on who in your life this device might genuinely help, and what you'd want to add for them specifically.
fields.buildLog: A photo of your finished Health Guard device and a note on your chosen priority rule.
fields.showFamily: PROJECT 3 COMPLETE: a working Health Guard device combining fall-alert and medicine-reminder features — a real health-tech idea the family can actually use.

sessions.title: Automatic Room Light — Light Sensing Revisited

fields.build: Build a real light-sensing circuit from an LDR and use it to automatically switch a room light on at dusk.
fields.components: Arduino UNO, breadboard, 1 LDR, 1× 10kΩ resistor, 1 LED (representing the room light), 1× 220Ω resistor, jumper wires.
fields.circuit: LDR and 10kΩ resistor in series between 5V and GND, midpoint to A0; LED on pin 8.
fields.experiment: Cover and uncover the LDR with your hand while watching the Serial Monitor, and test your own classroom's actual light levels at different times of day (lights on vs. off) to find a real threshold rather than guessing one.
fields.activity: Build the LDR voltage divider (the same principle taught in the AgriBot project's soil sensor) and wire the automatic-light logic.
fields.robotics: Automatic, condition-based behaviour — a light that switches on by itself at dusk — is one of the simplest and most genuinely useful forms of home-automation intelligence.
fields.engineering: Threshold calibration to a real environment: the 'correct' darkness level depends entirely on where the device is actually installed, and must be tested there, not assumed.
fields.electronics: The voltage-divider principle applied to light instead of soil moisture or a potentiometer — recognising that the same underlying circuit explains multiple different sensors.
fields.codeIt: Determine your own threshold value experimentally by testing real dark vs. light readings in your actual classroom.
fields.codeConcept: Reinforcement of analogRead() and if/else, now combined for the first time into a genuinely useful automation rule.
fields.codeReading: Given a specific threshold value, trace through what happens to the light for a sequence of readings across a simulated day (bright, dimming, dark, dawn).
fields.writeIt: Add a second threshold to create three light levels (bright/dim/dark) with three different responses, entirely on your own.
fields.miniChallenge: Calibrate your night-light so it switches on exactly when the classroom's overhead lights are switched off — a real, teacher-controlled test.
fields.debugging: A circuit with the LDR and resistor positions swapped inverts the behaviour (light triggers instead of dark) — reason out why rather than just swapping wires by trial and error.
fields.skills: Voltage-divider sensor design applied to a new context, real- environment threshold calibration, layered conditional logic.
fields.takeHome: Record what time your street's lights turn on for two evenings and note whether it's consistent.
fields.buildLog: A note on your chosen threshold and why it only works correctly in the room you tested it in.
fields.showFamily: A genuine automatic room light that switches on at dusk, calibrated by the student to the real home environment.

sessions.title: Sensing Temperature — Should the Fan Turn On?

fields.build: Wire and calibrate a thermistor-based temperature sensor, and use it to control a fan (represented by a small DC motor or LED indicator).
fields.components: Arduino UNO, breadboard, 1 thermistor, 1× 10kΩ resistor, small DC fan/motor or LED (as a stand-in), motor driver if using a real fan motor, jumper wires.
fields.circuit: Thermistor and 10kΩ resistor in series between 5V and GND, midpoint to analog pin A1; fan/motor wired through a driver as learned conceptually, or an LED stand-in on pin 9.
fields.experiment: Hold the thermistor gently between your fingers (or near, not touching, a warm object under supervision) and watch the analog reading change — discover that a thermistor is, again, just a variable resistor, this time reacting to temperature instead of light or soil moisture.
fields.activity: Build the thermistor voltage-divider circuit and confirm smooth, real-time temperature-related readings.
fields.robotics: Recognising the same voltage-divider principle appearing for a third time (soil, light, now temperature) — real engineers reuse understood building blocks rather than treating every new sensor as a mystery.
fields.engineering: Comfort-threshold design: unlike a simple dark/light cutoff, a 'is it too hot' threshold is genuinely a matter of comfort and context, and different users might reasonably want different thresholds — worth discussing explicitly.
fields.electronics: How a thermistor's resistance changes with temperature, and reading it exactly like any other voltage-divider sensor.
fields.codeIt: Print live temperature-related readings to the Serial Monitor while intentionally warming or cooling the sensor slightly.
fields.codeConcept: Full reuse of analogRead(), map(), and if/else — the week deliberately introduces no new syntax, only a new sensor, reinforcing that not every lesson needs new code concepts.
fields.codeReading: Given a temperature threshold and a set of readings, determine by hand when the fan should turn on and off.
fields.writeIt: Independently add a small 'hysteresis' gap (turn on above one value, only turn off below a slightly lower value) to stop the fan from rapidly clicking on and off right at the threshold — a genuine, practical engineering fix.
fields.miniChallenge: Demonstrate the fan/LED turning on when the sensor is warmed and off again once it cools, without rapid flickering at the threshold.
fields.debugging: A fan that rapidly clicks on and off is a classic threshold- oscillation bug — diagnose it as needing hysteresis, not a wiring fault.
fields.skills: Reapplying a known circuit principle to a third sensor type, comfort-threshold reasoning, hysteresis as a practical fix for oscillation.
fields.takeHome: Think of one home appliance that likely uses hysteresis (a thermostat, a fridge) and describe why it would click on and off constantly without it.
fields.buildLog: A note on the hysteresis gap you chose and why you picked that specific size.
fields.showFamily: A working temperature-triggered fan/light system that turns on smoothly without flickering.

sessions.title: PROJECT 4 BUILD: Smart Home Hub

fields.build: Combine light-sensing and temperature-sensing into one Smart Home Hub that manages both a room light and a fan, correctly handling both conditions at once.
fields.components: LDR (Week 11), thermistor (Week 12), LED (light) and fan/motor (from earlier weeks), Arduino UNO, breadboard, jumper wires.
fields.circuit: Full combination of Weeks 11 and 12 wiring, with a documented pin map covering both analog sensors and both outputs.
fields.experiment: Test the combined hub under four real conditions (dark+cool, dark+warm, bright+cool, bright+warm) and record its behaviour in each, discovering exactly where the combined logic does or doesn't do the right thing.
fields.activity: Assemble the complete two-sensor, two-output system on one breadboard.
fields.robotics: Real smart-home systems rarely rely on just one sensor — combining multiple readings and deciding what to do when they don't perfectly agree is a core home-automation design skill.
fields.engineering: Independent vs. combined logic: deciding whether the light and fan should be controlled completely independently, or whether one condition should ever override the other (e.g., should the fan run even in a dark room? Almost certainly yes) — a genuine design decision with a right answer this time, not just a preference.
fields.electronics: Managing two analog sensors and two outputs sharing the same Arduino board — pin planning as a real constraint.
fields.codeIt: Merge the Week 11 and Week 12 sketches into a single combined program, resolving how the two subsystems should (or shouldn't) interact.
fields.codeConcept: Structuring code with two independent decision blocks in one loop() — reinforcing that not every combination needs interlinked logic; sometimes two behaviours should just run side by side.
fields.codeReading: Trace through the combined code with a specific pair of sensor readings and predict both outputs' behaviour before testing.
fields.writeIt: Independently decide and implement whether your fan and light should ever interact (e.g., an 'away mode' that turns off the light regardless of darkness) — a fully open-ended, self- justified design choice.
fields.miniChallenge: Demonstrate the Smart Home Hub correctly handling all four test conditions, live, on demand.
fields.debugging: Working in pairs, test each other's hub with a condition you devise yourselves and report back any behaviour that doesn't seem right.
fields.skills: Multi-sensor, multi-output system integration, independent- vs-combined logic design, peer-driven testing.
fields.takeHome: Write a short explanation of any interaction you built between the light and fan, and why you decided it should (or shouldn't) work that way.
fields.buildLog: A photo of your finished Smart Home Hub and a note on what your partner's testing revealed about your design.
fields.showFamily: PROJECT 4 COMPLETE: a working two-sensor Smart Home Hub that manages a room's light and fan automatically, demonstrated live under real conditions.

sessions.title: Measuring Distance With Sound — The Parking Sensor

fields.build: Wire an ultrasonic distance sensor and use it to build a working 'parking sensor' that beeps faster as an object gets closer.
fields.components: Arduino UNO, breadboard, 1 HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor, 1 buzzer, jumper wires.
fields.circuit: HC-SR04 Trig pin to pin 9, Echo pin to pin 10, VCC to 5V, GND to GND; buzzer on pin 8.
fields.experiment: Measure the same fixed distance to a wall ten times in a row and notice the readings aren't perfectly identical each time — real sensors have real noise, which is why averaging several readings gives a more trustworthy value.
fields.activity: Wire the ultrasonic sensor and verify its readings against a physical tape measure for accuracy.
fields.robotics: Distance sensing using sound (exactly like how real car parking sensors and sonar work) is the foundation of almost all obstacle-avoidance and navigation behaviour in mobile robotics.
fields.engineering: Measurement noise and averaging: no real sensor gives a perfectly stable reading, and a robust design accounts for this instead of trusting a single sample.
fields.electronics: The ultrasonic sensor's separate Trigger and Echo pins, and measuring a time interval (how long sound takes to bounce back) rather than a voltage.
fields.codeIt: Write a sketch that takes five consecutive readings, stores them, and calculates the average.
fields.codeConcept: pulseIn(), the trigger-then-listen pattern, and a basic speed-of- sound distance calculation inside code.
fields.codeReading: Given a sample pulseIn() timing, calculate the expected distance by hand before checking it against the code's actual output.
fields.writeIt: Write a sketch, on your own, that makes the buzzer beep faster as an object gets closer — exactly like a real car's parking sensor.
fields.miniChallenge: Build a working 'parking sensor' calibrated against real measured distances, from 100cm down to 5cm.
fields.debugging: A sketch returning wildly wrong distances (far too large or negative) usually has the Trig/Echo pins mixed up — use your hand-calculation skill from the tracing exercise to find the mistake.
fields.skills: Sound-based distance measurement, data averaging for noise reduction, mapping continuous sensor data to a continuous output response.
fields.takeHome: Measure three real distances at home with a ruler (a doorway, a table height) so you can validate your sensor's accuracy next class.
fields.buildLog: A note on how close your sensor's readings were to your ruler measurements.
fields.showFamily: A working 'parking sensor' that beeps faster as a hand or object approaches — calibrated to real measured distances.

sessions.title: Real Power — Motors and Motor Drivers

fields.build: Discover, hands-on, why an Arduino pin cannot safely drive a DC motor directly, and correctly wire a real motor driver to control direction and speed.
fields.components: Arduino UNO, breadboard, 1 DC motor, 1 L298N (or L293D) motor driver module, external battery pack, jumper wires.
fields.circuit: Motor driver IN1/IN2 to pins 5/6, PWM enable to pin 9; driver's motor-power input to the external battery; Arduino GND, driver GND, and battery GND all connected together.
fields.experiment: Watch a brief, instructor-only, current-limited demonstration of what happens when a motor is wired directly to a digital pin — then wire the correct driver circuit yourselves and confirm safe operation.
fields.activity: Wire the complete motor-driver circuit and test forward, reverse, and stop.
fields.robotics: DC motors are the most common source of continuous motion in mobile robots and real vehicles alike — controlling them correctly is a foundational robotics-electronics skill.
fields.engineering: Power budgeting: recognising that different components need very different amounts of current, and routing the right amount of power to each part safely.
fields.electronics: Why microcontroller pins can't supply enough current for a motor, what an H-bridge driver does (allows direction reversal and higher current from a separate supply), and why a shared ground between the Arduino and the motor's power supply is critical.
fields.codeIt: Write a sketch that runs the motor forward for 2 seconds, stops, reverses for 2 seconds, stops.
fields.codeConcept: Using two digital pins to set motor direction and analogWrite() (PWM) on a third pin to control speed.
fields.codeReading: Given a motor-driver sketch, work out which HIGH/LOW combination on the direction pins means forward, reverse, and stop — a small truth table.
fields.writeIt: Write a sketch, independently, that gradually speeds the motor up from stopped to full speed over 3 seconds.
fields.miniChallenge: Reach three distinguishable speeds (slow/medium/fast) and find the minimum PWM value that still reliably starts the motor from rest.
fields.debugging: A very common real fault: no common ground between the Arduino and the battery pack — the motor simply won't respond, and this specific, easily-missed mistake is exactly what to check first.
fields.skills: Motor-driver wiring, direction and speed control, understanding current/power limits, common-ground troubleshooting.
fields.takeHome: Ask a family member with a car or an appliance about one device with a motor that needs to reverse direction, and note what it is.
fields.buildLog: A note on what would have happened if you'd wired the motor directly to the Arduino pin, and why.
fields.showFamily: A DC motor the student can start, stop, reverse, and speed up on command — the first genuinely powered mechanism in the course.

sessions.title: Building the Car — Chassis and Drivetrain

fields.build: Design, assemble, and test a real two-wheel-drive car chassis, treating the mechanical build itself as genuine engineering, not just a craft step.
fields.components: Two DC motors (Week 15), 2 wheels, 1 caster/ball-wheel, chassis material (acrylic or sturdy cardboard/plywood), motor driver, Arduino UNO, battery pack, fasteners.
fields.circuit: Both motors wired to the motor driver as in Week 15, now scaled to two motors (IN1-IN4 and two PWM enable pins).
fields.experiment: Command the assembled chassis to drive 'straight' for two metres and measure how far it drifts sideways — then investigate whether wheel alignment, motor mounting, or weight balance explains the drift.
fields.activity: Assemble the chassis: mount both motors symmetrically, attach wheels and caster, mount the Arduino and driver board, route wiring cleanly.
fields.robotics: A robot's software can only be as good as the physical body it runs on — a misaligned wheel or wobbly frame defeats even perfect code, exactly as it would in a real car.
fields.engineering: Mechanical precision and weight distribution: physical build quality directly affects performance, and 'the code is right but it still doesn't drive straight' is a completely legitimate engineering situation.
fields.electronics: Verifying the same motor-driver wiring from Week 15 survives being mounted on a moving chassis (strain relief, secure connectors).
fields.codeIt: Re-upload the Week 15 forward/reverse/speed sketch unchanged, to test the assembled chassis with identical code.
fields.codeConcept: No new syntax this week — deliberately, to keep this week's learning focused on mechanics, proving that identical code can behave differently depending on build quality.
fields.codeReading: Trace through your own build log from the previous two weeks to confirm all wiring matches your intended plan before final assembly.
fields.writeIt: Independently diagnose and mechanically correct your own chassis's straight-line drift, using only the measurement experiment as evidence, no teacher help.
fields.miniChallenge: Achieve less than 10cm of sideways drift over a 2-metre straight-line test using mechanical adjustment only.
fields.debugging: A chassis that curves in a J-shape usually has a loose wheel or misaligned motor mount — isolate this as a mechanical, not electrical, fault using process of elimination.
fields.skills: Mechanical assembly and alignment, systematic mechanical fault diagnosis, recognising that code-correct and system- correct aren't the same thing.
fields.takeHome: Sketch your chassis from three angles in your build log, labelling every mounted part.
fields.buildLog: A photo of your assembled car and a note on what actually caused your drift, since the code never changed.
fields.showFamily: A physical two-wheeled robot car that drives forward in a reasonably straight line.

sessions.title: PROJECT 5 BUILD: Park Assist — Auto-Brake Car

fields.build: Combine the ultrasonic parking sensor and the driving chassis into a complete car that senses an obstacle ahead and brakes itself automatically.
fields.components: Complete Week 16 chassis, motor driver, ultrasonic sensor (Week 14), Arduino UNO, battery pack.
fields.circuit: Full combination of the motor-driver wiring and the ultrasonic sensor wiring on one chassis, with a documented complete pin map.
fields.experiment: Test the car at three different approach speeds toward an obstacle and measure the stopping distance at each speed, discovering that faster driving needs either a longer sensing range or an earlier braking point — a genuine automotive safety trade-off.
fields.activity: Mount the ultrasonic sensor securely at the front of the car, facing directly forward, and finalize all wiring for a moving vehicle.
fields.robotics: This is the course's first true sense-decide-act robot: the car drives, continuously senses distance ahead, and brakes itself before collision — the foundational architecture of almost all reactive robotics, mirroring real automotive auto-braking systems.
fields.engineering: Speed vs. reaction-distance trade-off: a real design decision every self-driving or driver-assist system has to make, now explored with a real car the student built.
fields.electronics: Powering an ultrasonic sensor and a motor driver on the same car at once, verifying no electrical interference between them.
fields.codeIt: Merge the Week 14 ultrasonic-sensing code and Week 15/16 motor-driving code into one continuous sense-and-brake loop.
fields.codeConcept: Combining a previously-separate sensing sketch and a previously-separate motor sketch into one loop() — the biggest single code-merging exercise so far.
fields.codeReading: Trace through the combined loop with a specific sequence of simulated distance readings (100cm, 60cm, 30cm, 10cm) and predict the car's motor state at each point.
fields.writeIt: Independently make the braking distance adjustable via a variable (not a hard-coded number), and justify your chosen safety margin using this week's speed-vs-stopping-distance data.
fields.miniChallenge: Demonstrate the car reliably braking before hitting a wall from three different approach speeds, live, on demand.
fields.debugging: A car that brakes too late or crashes despite correct code often has the sensor mounted at a slight angle (reading the floor instead of the wall) — a mechanical, not code, issue, reinforcing Week 16's lesson.
fields.skills: Full sense-decide-act system integration, speed/braking trade- off reasoning, combined mechanical-electrical-software debugging.
fields.takeHome: Write a short note on what would need to change in your code if you wanted the car to reverse away from the obstacle instead of just stopping.
fields.buildLog: A photo/clip of Park Assist braking itself before a wall, with your chosen safety margin and why.
fields.showFamily: PROJECT 5 COMPLETE: a real, physical robot car that drives and automatically brakes itself before a collision — the family's first true 'robot,' not just a circuit.

sessions.title: Detecting Motion — The PIR Sensor

fields.build: Wire a PIR (passive infrared) motion sensor and use it to trigger an alert the instant someone walks past.
fields.components: Arduino UNO, breadboard, 1 PIR motion sensor module, 1 buzzer, 1 LED, jumper wires.
fields.circuit: PIR sensor's output pin to Arduino pin 2, VCC to 5V, GND to GND; buzzer on pin 8, LED on pin 9.
fields.experiment: Walk past the sensor at different distances and speeds, and stand very still nearby, to discover exactly what kind of motion the sensor does and doesn't detect — it senses heat- signature movement, not simply 'a person being present.'
fields.activity: Mount the PIR sensor at a fixed height facing an open walkway area, and wire the buzzer/LED alert.
fields.robotics: Motion detection is the core sensing principle behind most real home and commercial security systems — this is genuinely the same underlying technology, at a smaller scale.
fields.engineering: Detection range and field of view: like the ultrasonic sensor, a PIR sensor has real physical limits (angle, distance, warm-up time) that a good design must be tested against, not assumed.
fields.electronics: How a PIR sensor detects infrared heat changes in its field of view (conceptually, not circuit-internally) and outputs a simple HIGH/LOW signal the Arduino can read directly.
fields.codeIt: Write a sketch that sounds the alarm the instant motion is detected and prints a timestamp (using millis()) of when it happened.
fields.codeConcept: Reapplying digitalRead() and millis() (from the Health Guard project) to log exactly when an event occurred, not just react to it.
fields.codeReading: Given a printed log of PIR trigger timestamps, calculate the time gaps between triggers and discuss whether they suggest one person walking back and forth, or several separate events.
fields.writeIt: Independently add a short 'ignore additional triggers for X seconds' cooldown so a single walk-past doesn't spam the alarm repeatedly.
fields.miniChallenge: Correctly detect a person walking past at normal speed from across the room, without false-triggering from a stationary object.
fields.debugging: A PIR sensor that seems to trigger randomly with nobody nearby is often reacting to warm air currents (a fan, sunlight through a window) — a real-world lesson that sensors detect exactly what they detect, not what we assume they detect.
fields.skills: New sensor integration, event timestamping, cooldown logic to prevent alert-spamming.
fields.takeHome: Think of two places at home where a motion sensor would make sense, and two places where it would trigger constantly by mistake (near a window, near a fan).
fields.buildLog: A note on the exact conditions that did and didn't trigger your sensor.
fields.showFamily: A working motion-triggered alarm the student can demonstrate, including the cooldown feature.

sessions.title: Armed or Disarmed — Your First State Machine

fields.build: Build an arm/disarm system so the alarm only reacts to motion when the user has actually turned it on — a genuine security-system behaviour.
fields.components: Arduino UNO, breadboard, PIR sensor (Week 18), 1 pushbutton (arm/disarm switch), buzzer, LED, jumper wires.
fields.circuit: Button on pin 3 (as an arm/disarm toggle), PIR sensor on pin 2, buzzer on pin 8, status LED on pin 9 (lit = armed).
fields.experiment: Toggle the system between armed and disarmed while walking past the sensor each time, and confirm the alarm only ever sounds while armed — a simple but important real security-system behaviour to verify directly.
fields.activity: Wire the arm/disarm button alongside the existing PIR/buzzer/LED circuit.
fields.robotics: Many real robots and devices don't just react to sensors — they have distinct modes (armed/disarmed, on/off, day/night) that change how the same sensor reading is interpreted.
fields.engineering: State machines: representing a system's current 'mode' explicitly in code (as a variable) so behaviour correctly depends on both the current mode and the current sensor reading, not the sensor reading alone.
fields.electronics: No new wiring principle — full reuse of the debounced- button wiring from Project 1, applied to a new purpose (a mode switch instead of a toggle light).
fields.codeIt: Write a sketch where the button toggles an 'armed' boolean variable, and the PIR sensor's alarm logic only runs when that variable is true.
fields.codeConcept: Using a named state variable (e.g., bool isArmed) to control which code actually executes — the clearest introduction yet to 'code that behaves differently depending on mode.'
fields.codeReading: Given a sequence of button presses and PIR triggers, trace through exactly when the alarm should and shouldn't sound.
fields.writeIt: Independently add a short arming delay (e.g., 5 seconds after pressing arm before the sensor becomes active) so you have time to leave the room — exactly like a real home alarm.
fields.miniChallenge: Demonstrate correctly arming, walking away during the delay without triggering the alarm, and then having it correctly trigger once armed.
fields.debugging: An alarm that ignores the armed/disarmed state entirely usually has the state variable check misplaced or missing from the alarm logic — trace the code to find exactly where the check should have been.
fields.skills: State-machine thinking, mode-dependent behaviour, arming- delay logic.
fields.takeHome: Ask a family member how their (or a friend's) real home alarm system behaves when arming it, and compare it to what you built.
fields.buildLog: A note on why a state variable was necessary here, when earlier projects didn't need one.
fields.showFamily: A working arm/disarm security system with a realistic arming delay.

sessions.title: PROJECT 6 BUILD: Sentinel — The Complete Security System

fields.build: Finalize a complete Sentinel security system combining motion detection, arm/disarm state, cooldown, and a clear status indicator.

fields.robotics: Servos provide precise position control — exactly the mechanism needed for a lid that must open to a specific angle and stay there, unlike a continuously-spinning motor.

sessions.title: Feeling Instead of Hearing — Haptic Feedback

fields.build: Wire a small vibration motor and control its intensity with PWM, discovering why haptic (touch-based) feedback is sometimes better than sound.
fields.components: Arduino UNO, breadboard, 1 small vibration motor (coin/pancake type), 1 transistor (e.g., 2N2222) or a simple driver module, 1 diode (flyback protection), jumper wires.
fields.circuit: Vibration motor driven through a transistor switched by pin 9 (PWM-capable), with a flyback diode across the motor for protection, exactly as a small motor requires.
fields.experiment: Try wearing or holding the vibration motor while a partner reads aloud at the same time — notice how a vibration is easy to sense privately and without being distracted by ambient sound, unlike a buzzer everyone in the room can hear.
fields.activity: Wire the vibration motor with its protective diode and confirm safe, PWM-controlled operation at several intensities.
fields.robotics: Assistive technology often deliberately avoids sound-based alerts, since they can be missed in noisy environments or draw unwanted public attention — haptic feedback is a genuinely important, real accessibility-design choice.
fields.engineering: Designing for a specific user's real needs, not a generic 'average' user: a device meant to be worn discreetly by someone who is visually impaired has different, real design requirements than a classroom demo buzzer.
fields.electronics: Why a small motor needs a flyback diode (to protect the transistor from voltage spikes when the motor turns off) — a genuinely new, important circuit-protection concept.
fields.codeIt: Write a sketch that ramps the vibration motor's intensity up and down smoothly using analogWrite(), and test at what PWM value the motor first becomes noticeably strong enough to feel.

fields.skills: Haptic actuator control, transistor-driven motor switching, circuit protection (flyback diodes), user-centred design thinking.
fields.takeHome: Ask a family member to close their eyes and try to tell apart three vibration intensities you create, and record how accurate they were.
fields.buildLog: A note on which vibration pattern your blindfolded test partner found easiest to understand, and why you think that was.

sessions.title: Sensing Rising Water — A DIY Water-Level Probe

fields.build: Build a simple, low-cost water-level sensor from bare wire probes and calibrate it against real rising water.
fields.components: Arduino UNO, breadboard, 2-3 bare wire probes (or a purpose-made water-level sensor strip), 1× 10kΩ resistor, a small clear container, water, jumper wires.
fields.circuit: One probe to 5V, a second (or several, at increasing heights) to analog pin A0 through a 10kΩ pull-down resistor to GND — water conducts electricity between the probes, closing the circuit as it rises.
fields.experiment: Slowly pour water into the container and watch the analog reading jump the moment water bridges the two probes, then test with probes at two different heights to sense two distinct water levels.
fields.activity: Mount 2-3 probes at different heights inside a small container to test 'low water,' 'rising,' and 'critical' levels.
fields.robotics: Water-level detection is a foundational sensor in flood- warning and disaster-management systems — this simple probe is the same underlying principle used in real, larger- scale flood sensors.
fields.engineering: Tiered detection: rather than one single 'wet or dry' reading, using probes at multiple heights gives useful, staged information (rising, but not yet critical) — a real, important disaster-warning design pattern.
fields.electronics: Water (especially with any dissolved minerals) conducts electricity well enough to complete a simple circuit — the same voltage-divider principle as the soil sensor, applied to standing water instead.
fields.codeIt: Print live readings from each probe height to the Serial Monitor while slowly raising the water level.
fields.codeConcept: Reading and comparing multiple analog/digital inputs together (multiple probes at once) to determine a staged water level, rather than a single simple threshold.
fields.codeReading: Given readings from three probes at different heights, determine by hand which stage (safe/rising/critical) the water is currently at.
fields.writeIt: Independently write the logic that reports the water's current stage (not just wet/dry) based on which probes are currently triggered.
fields.miniChallenge: Correctly identify and report all three water stages as you slowly raise real water in the test container.
fields.debugging: A probe reading that never changes even when submerged usually indicates a poor or corroded contact point — a real, physical maintenance lesson relevant to any real-world water sensor.
fields.skills: DIY sensor construction from bare components, tiered/staged sensing, disaster-relevant sensor design.
fields.takeHome: Research (with a parent if needed) one real example of a flood-warning system used in an Indian city or river system.
fields.buildLog: A note on the water levels (in centimetres) that triggered each of your probes.
fields.showFamily: A working, homemade water-level sensor that correctly reports rising water in stages.

sessions.title: When to Whisper and When to Shout — Escalating Alerts

fields.components: Water-level probes (Week 27), gas sensor (reused from Clean City), 1 buzzer, 2 LEDs (yellow = warning, red = critical), Arduino UNO, breadboard.
fields.circuit: Water probes on analog/digital pins as in Week 27, gas sensor on A1 (as in Clean City), buzzer on pin 8, yellow LED on pin 9, red LED on pin 10.
fields.experiment: Compare how it feels to hear a single, identical alarm tone for both 'water is rising a little' and 'water is about to flood the room' versus a genuinely different, escalating pattern for each — discovering directly why real emergency systems use tiered signals.
fields.activity: Wire the combined water and gas sensing with two distinct alert levels (steady yellow LED and slow beep for warning; flashing red LED and fast/continuous beep for critical).
fields.robotics: Real disaster-warning systems (tsunami sirens, fire alarms, flood warnings) use genuinely different signal patterns for different severity levels — a single generic 'alarm sound' actually communicates less useful information.
fields.engineering: Escalation design: deciding exactly which sensor readings, from either the water probes or the gas sensor, count as 'warning' versus 'critical,' and making sure the two severity levels are unmistakably different to a person hearing or seeing them.
fields.electronics: No new wiring concept — full combination of two previously separate multi-level sensing circuits (water-level and gas) with a genuinely tiered dual-LED and buzzer-pattern output.
fields.codeIt: Write code where warning-level conditions produce a slow, steady alert pattern, and critical-level conditions produce a distinctly faster, more urgent pattern.
fields.codeConcept: Structuring code with multiple named alert-level functions (soundWarning(), soundCritical()) chosen based on the combined sensor state — reinforcing modular, purpose- named code.
fields.codeReading: Given a specific combination of water and gas readings, determine which alert level (none/warning/critical) the code should currently be in.
