fields.debugging: A rover that gets stuck oscillating in front of an obstacle (turning back and forth without progressing) needs its detour logic adjusted — a genuine, common real-robotics bug worth experiencing directly.
fields.skills: Multi-sensor priority-based decision-making, detour-and- recover behaviour design.
fields.takeHome: Sketch, in your build log, the detour path you'd want your rover to take around a specific obstacle shape.
fields.buildLog: A note on how many attempts it took to get a reliable detour- and-rejoin behaviour working.
fields.showFamily: A rover that follows a path and correctly detours around an obstacle before rejoining its route.

sessions.title: Smoother Driving — Proportional Path Correction

fields.build: Move beyond simple on/off path-following to smooth, proportional correction — 'how much to turn,' not just 'which way' — for genuinely faster, smoother rover driving.
fields.components: Existing rover build (Weeks 30-31), full IR sensor array using analog readings.
fields.circuit: Unchanged from Week 30, now using all sensor channels for a weighted error calculation.
fields.experiment: Run the rover with simple on/off path-following first and watch it wobble and overshoot on curves, then compare it against a version that calculates 'how far off centre' the path is and turns proportionally — feeling the difference directly.
fields.activity: No new build — this week is entirely about improving the driving algorithm on the existing rover.
fields.robotics: Smooth, precise rover motion requires knowing not just which direction is wrong but how wrong, and correcting proportionally — the same core idea behind real robotics and automotive control systems.
fields.engineering: Proportional control, introduced entirely through hands-on tuning and comparison rather than a mathematical lecture — matching the course's build-first philosophy even for a genuinely advanced idea.
fields.electronics: Full reinforcement of PWM motor-speed control, now applied continuously and dynamically rather than at fixed preset speeds.
fields.codeIt: First test the 'how far off centre' error calculation alone (printed to Serial Monitor while manually moving the sensor bar over the path) before connecting it to the motors.
fields.codeConcept: Computing a weighted error value from multiple analog sensor readings, and using it (multiplied by a chosen constant) to set a proportional speed difference between the two motors.
fields.codeReading: Given a specific error value and proportional constant, calculate by hand what speed difference should apply to the two motors, then verify against the real code.
fields.writeIt: Independently experiment with at least three different proportional constants on the real track and record which produces the smoothest run.
fields.miniChallenge: Complete a full lap of the test path with visibly smoother, faster motion than the on/off version, and state your chosen constant and why.
fields.debugging: A rover that overcorrects violently (a much bigger wobble than the simple version) almost always has its proportional constant set too high — a specific, recognisable symptom-to- cause relationship.
fields.skills: Continuous error calculation, proportional-control tuning through systematic experimentation.
fields.takeHome: Explain in your own words (using a driving or cycling analogy) why 'turn a little when a little off course, a lot when a lot off course' works better than always turning hard.
fields.buildLog: A note comparing your best on/off lap and your best proportional lap with real data (time, number of wobbles).
fields.showFamily: A visibly smoother, faster rover, with the student able to explain the specific tuning decision responsible.

sessions.title: PROJECT 10 BUILD & MISSION DAY: Unknown Terrain Challenge

fields.build: Finalize the Mars Rover and test it, for the first time, on a genuinely unknown terrain layout revealed only on Mission Day — a celebratory event, not an exam.
fields.components: Complete rover build: chassis, motor driver, IR sensor array, ultrasonic sensor, Arduino UNO, battery pack.
fields.circuit: Finalized combination of all Project 10 wiring, fully documented with a clean pin map.
fields.experiment: On Mission Day, the actual path-and-obstacle layout is revealed for the first time — a genuinely different, previously-unseen arrangement from anything tested in Weeks 30-32 — and each rover gets to attempt it live.
fields.activity: Final build clean-up and reliability check before Mission Day: secure wiring, confirm the sensor array and ultrasonic sensor are firmly mounted for a real, unrehearsed run.
fields.robotics: This is the ultimate proof of everything Project 10 taught: a rover built through genuine understanding of path-following, obstacle-avoidance, and proportional control will handle unknown terrain far better than one that was simply tuned to memorize one specific practiced layout.
fields.engineering: Designing for robustness under real uncertainty — deliberately building a rover that performs well across a range of conditions, not just one perfectly memorized test course, mirrored directly in Mission Day's genuine reveal-on-the-day format.
fields.electronics: Full and final reliability verification of every wire and connection under real, unrehearsed, one-shot conditions.
fields.codeIt: No new practice this week — full, live application of everything built in Weeks 30-32.
fields.codeConcept: Full consolidation of arrays, compound conditionals, and proportional control into one final, complete rover program.
fields.codeReading: Before Mission Day, do a final self-review of your own code and make sure you can explain every function to a teammate, cold, without notes.
fields.writeIt: The Mission Day run itself is the ultimate independent challenge — no code copying, no advance knowledge of the terrain, no last-minute help.
fields.miniChallenge: Complete as much of the actual, unseen Mission Day terrain as possible — partial success is celebrated, not just a perfect run.
fields.debugging: If something goes wrong mid-run, small on-the-spot adjustments are allowed (not a full rebuild) — a realistic, low-pressure version of real robotics field troubleshooting.
fields.skills: Full autonomous system integration, genuine performance under real uncertainty, composure under a live, unrehearsed test.
fields.takeHome: Write an honest note on what surprised you about the real Mission Day terrain and what you'd tweak with one more week.
fields.buildLog: A photo/clip of your rover's actual Mission Day run — celebrate the attempt, whatever the outcome.
fields.showFamily: PROJECT 10 COMPLETE: a fully autonomous rover, tested live on genuinely unknown terrain — Mission Day is a fun, celebratory event families are warmly invited to watch.

sessions.title: Pick Your Problem — Planning Your Own Invention

fields.build: Choose and clearly define a genuine real-world problem to solve, and plan which sensors, actuators, and skills from the last nine projects you'll need.
fields.components: None prescribed this week — planning only.
fields.circuit: N/A this week — to be designed by the student based on their chosen invention.
fields.experiment: Do a small piece of real research relevant to your chosen problem (e.g., if choosing a plant-related idea, actually check how a real plant at home behaves) before finalizing your plan.
fields.activity: No build yet — this week is entirely about defining a clear, real problem and sketching your planned approach.
fields.robotics: The final and most authentic test of everything learned is not solving a problem someone else fully defined, but picking, scoping, and justifying a real problem worth solving in the first place.
fields.engineering: Needs analysis: a poorly defined problem can't be well solved no matter how good your technical skills are — this is the true first step of any real invention.
fields.electronics: Reviewing, from memory, every sensor and circuit type covered across the ten prior projects, to decide which ones your invention might need.
fields.codeIt: Sketch (in plain language, not code yet) what your invention should sense, decide, and do.
fields.codeConcept: No new syntax — full, independent selection from everything already learned, based on what your own invention actually needs.
fields.codeReading: Review and reread your own strongest previous project's code (your choice) to confirm you genuinely understand it before planning to reuse or adapt any of it.
fields.writeIt: Independently write a short, clear one-paragraph description of your invention and defend, in writing, why it's a problem worth solving.
fields.miniChallenge: Present your plan to another student or pair and get one honest piece of feedback before finalizing it.
fields.debugging: N/A this week — planning only.
fields.skills: Independent problem identification, real needs-based research, project planning.
fields.takeHome: Ask one real potential user of your idea (a family member, if it's home-based) whether they'd actually find it useful, and note their honest answer, even if it's critical.
fields.buildLog: Your written problem statement and initial plan, kept as the first entry of your Capstone build log.
fields.showFamily: A clear, research-backed plan for the student's own original invention.

sessions.title: Build Your Invention

fields.build: Build a first working version of your own invention, drawing on any skill or component from the entire course.
fields.components: Student-selected combination of any components used across Projects 1-10, plus any small new addition, approved as needed.
fields.circuit: Fully student-designed, documented in the build log with a clean pin map.
fields.experiment: If your invention needs a sensor you haven't calibrated before, run a quick isolated test of it first — exactly the same 'test before integrating' habit used in Project 1's very first LED circuit.
fields.activity: Build your invention, with your instructor available for help only when you ask for it — this is genuinely your project.
fields.robotics: This week represents the fullest transfer of ownership in the whole course — the instructor is a helper you can call on, not a director telling you each next step.
fields.engineering: Full, independent application of the build-test-fix cycle used in every prior project, now entirely self-directed.
fields.electronics: Independent circuit design and wiring for your own specific chosen components.
fields.codeIt: Write your invention's first working code draft, asking for help only on the specific parts you're stuck on.
fields.codeConcept: Full, independent selection and combination of any Arduino C/C++ concept from the entire course.
fields.codeReading: If working in a pair, explain your code sections to each other so both of you understand the whole program, not just the parts you personally wrote.
fields.writeIt: Resolve at least one real design problem (something that doesn't behave as expected) without your instructor solving it for you.
fields.miniChallenge: Get one genuine, even if partial, working demonstration of your invention's core idea by the end of this week.
fields.debugging: Apply the full isolate-before-fixing method used throughout the course, asking your instructor to confirm your diagnosis rather than to hand you the answer.
fields.skills: Full independent build, cross-team code understanding, self- directed problem-solving.
fields.takeHome: Update your build log with what currently works, what doesn't yet, and what you're planning to try next.
fields.buildLog: A photo of your invention's current state and an honest note on what's working and what isn't.
fields.showFamily: A partially working, genuinely original invention addressing a real problem the family may already know about.

sessions.title: FINAL SHOWCASE — Your Invention, Your Way

fields.build: Finish, refine, and publicly show off your own original invention at the course's Final Showcase — a celebration, not an exam.
fields.components: Complete, finished Capstone invention.
fields.circuit: Final, fully documented circuit in the build log.
fields.experiment: Run your own invention through a simple test you design yourself, at least five times, to make sure it works reliably before showcase day.
fields.activity: Final build refinement, wiring clean-up, and simple presentation preparation for the showcase.
fields.robotics: The Final Showcase is a public celebration of everything built across all ten projects and your own capstone invention — a demo day, like a real maker fair, not a viva or exam.
fields.engineering: Presenting your own work confidently and honestly, including what you're proud of and what you'd still like to improve — genuine engineering pride, not performance anxiety.
fields.electronics: Final wiring check and clean-up for a reliable, repeatable live demonstration.
fields.codeIt: No new code practice — full, final demonstration of your own independently written program.
fields.codeConcept: Full and final demonstration of code you wrote, understand, and can explain in your own words.
fields.codeReading: If someone at the showcase (a parent, another student) asks how a part of your invention works, you should be able to explain it simply and clearly, because you built it and you understand it.
fields.writeIt: Your finished, working invention and your ability to talk about it confidently is the final challenge of the whole course.
fields.miniChallenge: Successfully demonstrate your invention's core behaviour at the showcase.
fields.debugging: If something goes wrong live at the showcase, stay calm and explain what's happening out loud — a real engineer talking through a real hiccup is impressive, not embarrassing.
fields.skills: Public demonstration, confident and honest explanation of your own original work — the complete set of skills built across the entire course, on display.
fields.takeHome: None — course complete. Enjoy the showcase.
fields.buildLog: A final photo of your invention at the showcase, and one sentence on what you're most proud of.
fields.showFamily: FINAL SHOWCASE: a public celebration where every family sees an original, working invention their child designed, built, coded, and can proudly explain — the true, unmistakable proof of everything learned.
